source.title: SafeKey: Amplifying Aha-Moment Insights for Safety Reasoning
source.authors: Kai-Qing Zhou; Xuandong Zhao; Gao-Wen Liu; Jayanth Srinivasa; Ao-Song Feng; D. Song; X. Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates harmfulness under a prefilling attack and measures per-token KL divergence between base and safety-aligned models. These are conceptual tests of V4 and V3, not reproductions of the original fine-tuning interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests prefilling and plots per-token KL divergence. Its safety fine-tuning is intended to improve safety, not to test whether harmful-example or ordinary benign fine-tuning erodes it. The key-sentence prevalence and attention analyses do not measure a claim version's named outcome. The study also evaluates whether query summaries convey safety, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study runs a prefilling attack (20 harmful-response tokens) on R1-distilled reasoning models before and after safety SFT. These are a new model class and setting for V4. Table 1 also gives unprefilled harmfulness on the source prompt sets (StrongReject, JBB), which serves as an approximate baseline. Figure 7 plots per-token KL bearing on V3, but the curve cannot be read numerically.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SFT-aligned reasoning models fail to generalize to unseen jailbreaks, and that SafeKey strengthens the key-sentence safety 'aha moment', lowering harmfulness while keeping general ability. They acknowledge limits on multi-turn attacks and over-refusal, and note the method's restriction to reasoning models.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains reasoning models on safety data with auxiliary safety-head and query-mask objectives; it does not reproduce either original fine-tuning intervention or the original shallow-safety analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported prefilling harmfulness rates differ by model size and training variant. The paper also reports different KL curves for 7B and 8B models, but does not provide their values in text.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4o (59.9%) and R1-8B SFT (80.4%) judged query safety from the model's query-understanding text alone. The 148 excerpts came from successfully jailbroken responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning models' query-understanding text carries safety information the model fails to use when answering.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeKey shows higher KL from the base model than SFT at all positions up to 50 and lower prefill harmfulness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training that raises deviation from base beyond early tokens coincides with better prefill robustness (own-method, V7-adjacent).

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The per-token KL values are shown only in a figure, and the text does not specify their early-position concentration. Prefilling results have no matched no-prefill comparison. Safety evaluation relies primarily on GPT-4o judgments, although the appendix reports a 92% human agreement rate on sampled cases.
record.rows_left_out: No results on harmful-example or benign-data safety erosion were reported. Other safety benchmark outcomes evaluate safety-improving training rather than the interventions in V1 or V2. No additional rows were omitted for the row limit.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning erosion test. The safety SFT reduces harm rather than eroding it.
Whether KL concentrates in the first few tokens; the plot cannot be read numerically.
Suffix (GCG) attacks and decoding changes; a matched no-prefill rate on the exact prefill query set.
No explicit deepening method. SafeKey's higher KL across positions plus lower prefill harm is own-method evidence and is not framed as deepening.

missing.what: Unprefilled harmfulness on StrongReject/JBB per model, needed as the approximate V4 baseline
Prefill harmfulness rate and score for the DPSH-only and QMM-only ablations (e.g., 14B: 18.2→10.7 with QMM only)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: the study puts reasoning models in a new setting rather than using a different method on the original question. The prefill set was built from R1-8B's own harmful completions, so baselines for the R1-Distilled rows are confounded. Harm is judged by GPT-4o, counting only score 5; the authors report 92% agreement with human labels on 100 samples.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on harmful examples causes harmful compliance.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
The per-token KL is plotted, but the text does not state whether it is concentrated in the first few positions; plotted values are not reported numerically.
The paper tests prefill attacks, but not suffix attacks or decoding changes; it does not report a matched no-prefill comparison.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether the data or training objective causes safety shallowness.
Whether safety training spreads safety beyond the first tokens and whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: STAR-1 safety-SFT R1-distilled 7B/8B/14B under a 20-token harmful prefill
relationships.reason: Prefill raises harmfulness from ~0–3% unprefilled (StrongReject/JBB) to 18–30% (R6, R9, R12). Refusal is clearly bypassed, but only partially. The baseline is approximate, not matched.
relationships.display_finding: The prefill raised harmfulness from about 0–3% without prefill to 18–30%, a clear but partial bypass measured against an approximate, unmatched baseline.

source_check.condition: STAR-1 safety-SFT R1-distilled 7B/8B/14B under a 20-token harmful prefill
source_check.reason: R6/R9/R12 show incomplete bypass: 29.8%, 24.0%, and 18.2% harmfulness. Full-benchmark unprefilled rates are approximate comparisons; the exact prefill query set lacks a matched control.

relationships.reason: Prefill still raises harmfulness from ~0–1% to 7–17% (R7, R10, R13). The effect is weaker than for SFT, and the rows are the study's own method.
relationships.display_finding: On SafeKey-trained models, the study's own method, the prefill still raised harmfulness from about 0–1% to 7–17%, a weaker effect than after STAR-1 fine-tuning.
